▶ Chart key
Amber — the 200-week average. Four years of trading in one line: below it, a stock has historically been cheap. Blue — the 50-week average. A year of price: above it, the trend is up and intact; below it, the trend is broken. Violet — the weekly RSI. How stretched the price is — pushed too far, too fast, in either direction. Dashed lines mark 70 and 30: above 70, overbought; below 30, oversold. Teal — the P/E ratio. The price divided by the last twelve months of earnings per share — how many dollars investors pay for one dollar of profit. Where the line breaks, the company was losing money: there is no P/E without earnings. The dashed line is the stock's own median P/E: above it, expensive for itself; below it, cheap for itself. Grey — the 20-week volume average. Bars poking above it mean a heavy trading week; below it, a quiet one. Volume confirms a move: price rising on rising volume is healthy — rising on shrinking volume is tiring. Green and red dots — Johnny’s indicator. A green dot marks a buy day: the RSI at or under 30, the VIX at or over 25, the price at least 30% down from its highest price of the last two years and PEG at or under 1 — or, where PEG can’t be calculated, the price at least 40% down from its highest price of the last two years — all on the same day. A green dot also marks a buy day through the second door: the RSI at or under 30, the VIX at or over 25, the price at least 20% down from its highest price of the last two years, below its 200-week average and PEG at or under 2, all on the same day. Where PEG can’t be calculated, the second door does not open. A red dot marks a sell day: the RSI over 70, the VIX under 15, PEG at 2 or more and the price at least 50% above its 200-week average, all of it held for five straight days. The S&P 500, Nasdaq, gold, and Bitcoin have no PEG to calculate, so no PEG leg applies to them: the S&P 500 and Nasdaq buy at 25% down from the two-year high, gold and Bitcoin at 30% down — with the same RSI at or under 30 and the VIX at or over 25. A ringed green dot marks a day that scored 85 or higher on the 100-point score but did not pass the buy gate. A ringed dot in the buy green or the sell red marks a trade a member of Congress disclosed for that day — the bigger the ring, the bigger the disclosed amount (sized by the filed range’s midpoint, an estimate).

The chart opens on the S&P 500, Line, five-year view. Daily view carries the 200-day and 50-day averages and the daily RSI; Weekly view carries the same three by the week. A stock with under four years of trading history has no 200-day line yet; the note under the chart says so when that is the case.

How it works▶

STRC and SATS sit with the rest of the names, but their dots print on price alone: a buy dot when the close is in a buy zone — $99–$95, $95–$85 or $85–$70 — and they never sell.

Every green dot buys the Buy amount of that name at that day’s close; every red dot sells the Sell amount, never more than the position holds. Fractional shares, the way the big platforms allow them. The dots and the prices are the same ones the chart above draws, from the same daily file, so this portfolio can never disagree with the chart.

Prices are split-adjusted, so stock splits are already in the numbers. Dividends are not in the prices, and they are not counted anywhere in this run — every line is price only, so a stock’s value here dips on its ex-dividend day exactly as its price does.

The comparison is one line, set by the three controls above it. Compare against picks what it holds — the S&P 500, the Nasdaq, Gold, Bitcoin, Cash, or the two indexes half and half. It buys picks when its money goes in: the Amount on each of your buy-signal days, the Amount on the first trading day of each month or each week, or the whole Amount on the run’s first day. It never sells. Cash just piles its amounts up on the same schedule, and its gain is always zero — this page counts gains and losses, not purchasing power.

Trades execute at the close on the day the dot prints · no commissions or slippage · figures are before taxes · cash earns no interest.

How the rules are graded▶

Rules scored from this data — eight are scored from data and ten are graded by judgment (below); the rest of each framework is labelled “Principle” in the investor’s profile, never scored by proxy. Druckenmiller: Momentum > 0 (confirming only); Buffett: ROE ≥ 15%; Tepper: Growth ≥ 10%; Alden: ROE > 0 and Margin > 0; O’Shaughnessy: Momentum in the top 5 of the table — the table’s 3-month momentum stands in for his six-month momentum; Baker: PEG < 1.0 and less than half the median PEG of the expensive AI names (AAOI). Baker compared P/E, not PEG — this is the table’s PEG implementation of his P/E-gap test, not a threshold he stated. Lynch: fast growers only (growth ≥ 20%): PEG < 1.0 = pass, PEG ≥ 2.0 = fail; the rest of his checklist is graded with it — full list in his profile below. His rule uses expected growth; the score uses the table’s growth field. Buffett’s and Alden’s ROE legs are tested whenever the weekly fundamentals refresh carries the figures for that company, and show as not tested until it does. Graham: the Defensive Investor tests (The Intelligent Investor, ch. 14) — every testable test must pass and at least four of the seven must be testable; the full list is in his profile below. His 20-year dividend test can’t be checked from filings data, and financials aren’t graded on tests written for industrials. Graham’s leg, and the rest of Lynch’s checklist, test from the filings figures the updater writes alongside the fundamentals; until a run carries them, they show as not tested. Judgment grades — Marks, Klarman, Dalio, Thiel, Andreessen, Simons, Ives, Lavish, Sacks and Visser. Each column asks five questions from that investor’s own published work. Each answer comes from the evidence listed in the popover. The grades were judged on 2026-11-18 from the data then on this page. The verdict rules follow each method: Marks and Klarman must pass both of their gates (price vs value and permanent-loss risk; margin of safety and permanent-loss avoidance) and at least three of five questions; Thiel must pass all five, his own written standard; Andreessen (software eating an industry, an extreme strength), Ives (a central AI beneficiary), Lavish (an asset no one can print more of), Sacks (retention, gross margin) and Visser (a receiver of the AI capex) must pass their gates and at least three of five; Dalio and Simons have no gate and need at least three of five. Simons’ questions grade only whether a stock is the kind his documented machine can trade — his signals themselves are secret and are not graded. Their markers carry a dashed outline so a judgment is never mistaken for a measurement. The judgments live in this page, not in the nightly data file, and are re-judged deliberately rather than recomputed.

Every screen above must beat a low-cost total-market index fund after costs and taxes — if it can’t, own the index. (Bogle)

My checklist for any stock, in order — a stock has to clear each step to stay in.

Run one stock through my full checklist.

The runner and the review grade individual companies. An index, gold or Bitcoin has no earnings or return on equity to grade — for those, use The Chart above and its 200-week line.

  1. Step 0 — Big enough to trust: US-listed, worth $1B+, priced $10+, heavily traded.
  2. Step 1 — Cheap and strong: low price for its earnings, high returns on capital, little debt.
  3. Step 2 — Rank what’s left: best mix of cheapness, quality, cash flow, and momentum; keep the top 10–30.
  4. Step 3 — Read before buying: the company’s own filings and story, and only buy with a 25–50% safety margin.
  5. Step 4 — Protect the downside: risk at most 0.5–1% of the portfolio per stock; a 7–8% stop on momentum trades.
  6. Step 5 — Beat the index, or own it: if the picks can’t beat a total-market index fund after costs over 3–5 years, the index wins. (Bogle)
Full details — every rule and number▶

Thresholds are strict on purpose — if you get zero results, loosen one at a time (e.g. ROIC 12%, P/E 25). Data differs by platform (EBIT, EV, ROIC definitions) — compare 2–3 sources before trusting a single number. This is my system, built from the committee’s frameworks — not the committee’s consensus.

Step 0 — Universe (mine)

US-listed common stocks. Market cap $1B+; price $10+; average volume 500K+ shares. Exclude financials and utilities from the ROIC/EBIT steps; screen banks and insurers separately on P/B and ROE.

Step 1A — Value + quality screen

Cheap (Graham, Lynch): earnings yield (EBIT / EV) 8%+ — 8% is my cutoff. P/E 20 or less (strict Graham mode: 15 or less). P/B 3 or less (strict Graham: 1.5 or less; P/E × P/B 22.5 or less). PEG 1 or less (Lynch); under 0.5 is a standout.

Quality (Buffett): ROIC 15%+. ROE 15%+. Debt/equity 0.5 or less (mine); net debt / EBITDA 2 or less (mine). Free cash flow / net income 90%+. Gross margin 40%+ (mine). FCF yield 4%+ (mine). Positive earnings every year for the last 5 years (Graham uses 10).

Health: Piotroski F-score 7+ (mine — Piotroski’s own “strong” line is 8–9).

Step 2 — Rank the survivors

Sum the ranks (1 = best) for earnings yield, ROIC, FCF yield, and 12-month relative strength. Take the top 20–30, or the top 10 for a concentrated list. Cheap stocks often fail the trend rules — pick one lead style and use the other as confirmation.

Step 3 — Research before buying

Read the last 10-K and last earnings call. Why is it cheap or strong? Is the earnings drop or jump one-time? Check insider activity and share count trend (buybacks or dilution). Check debt maturity and cash flow. Estimate intrinsic value; buy only with a 25–50% margin of safety (Buffett/Klarman).

Step 4 — Risk rules

Entry for momentum names: breakout from a tight base on rising volume. Stop loss: 7–8% below entry for momentum trades; for value, use thesis-based exits (mine). Risk 0.5–1% of the portfolio per position (mine). Average loss should be well below the average gain. Rebalance value picks yearly (O’Shaughnessy).

Step 5 — Benchmark (Bogle)

Track results vs. a total-market index fund after taxes and fees. If you can’t beat it over 3–5 years, shift core money to the index. John Bogle’s Cost Matters Hypothesis: after costs, the average active investor must underperform a low-cost index fund by exactly the amount of the costs. SPIVA Year-End 2025: 89.5% of US large-cap funds underperformed after costs over 15 years; over 20 years, ~93–94% fell short. Buffett’s 2007–2017 bet proved the point: a Vanguard S&P 500 index fund compounded 7.1%/yr against hedge funds, after fees.

The Latest

PoliticianTickerTradeAmountTradedFiledLag

On the charts: a solid dot is Johnny’s indicator. A ringed dot is a politician’s disclosed trade on that day — a bigger ring means a bigger disclosed amount, sized by the range’s midpoint, which is an estimate. Buys sit on the buy side, sells on the sell side, the same as the indicator’s dots.

How this works — the law, the ranges, and the estimates

The STOCK Act (2012) requires members of Congress to disclose their stock trades — and their spouses’ and dependent children’s — within 45 days of the trade. So “the latest” here means the latest filed, not the latest traded: a trade can be weeks old on the day it appears, and the Lag column shows exactly how long it took.

Amounts are ranges because the law asks for ranges. The feed shows each range exactly as it was filed, never a single made-up number. Where one number is needed to add things up — the Most Watched ranking, the performance figures, the portfolio curves, the sizes of the chart dots — the middle of the range is used, and that figure is labelled an estimate.

Household trades file under the member’s name. Nancy Pelosi’s filings, for example, are her husband Paul’s trades, disclosed under her name as the law requires; each row notes whose account a trade was in when the filing says so.

The “since they bought” figures use this page’s own price data: for every disclosed buy the price file covers, the return from the trade date to the latest close, weighted by the size of each buy. A stock the price file does not cover shows its trades with no performance figure — no coverage, no number.

The small curve on a card is a reconstruction from that member’s disclosed trades, not their real account: each covered buy opens a position sized at its range midpoint at that day’s close, sells close the oldest positions first, and sales of positions opened before this window are left out. It answers one narrow question — what would these disclosed trades, and only these, have done?

Committees are shown because they are the context that makes a trade readable: the same defence-stock purchase is a different fact in the hands of an Armed Services member than in anyone else’s. The committees listed are the member’s current assignments, from the public congress-legislators dataset.

The 45-day deadline is the law’s, so a filing that took longer is flagged with how many days late it was — the dates themselves, stated plainly. This section is data only: filings, dates, ranges, and arithmetic on them. What any of it means is the reader’s call.

Two frameworks, one strategy. This tool is the cash framework: the VIX sets how much cash the portfolio holds — building toward 30% in cash as the VIX falls to 10, and deploying down to a 5% cash floor as the VIX rises to 35. The indicator on the price chart is the second framework: it picks when to buy and sell, and which stocks. The two build on each other — sell signals fill the cash first, and buy signals direct the cash back out. Build cash two ways: collect the daily dividends STRC and SATS pay, and sell stocks and index funds as the VIX falls toward low levels.

Entry

Promising — the fundamentals are strong: earnings growth · return on capital · margins · a strong balance sheet · cash in hand · network effects.

The Investment Committee Stock Review, Johnny’s Stock Checklist, and The Chart help find good entries.

Promising and undervalued
Risk

Not investing is the riskiest move of all: money that never gets invested loses purchasing power every year and falls behind the hurdle rate. The base comes first — the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, Bitcoin, STRC, and SATS — and promising stocks are added on top, never instead. What the skeptics are picturing isn’t investing; it’s trading, speculating, gambling.

Once you’re in, the discipline flips: trim a holding when it becomes overvalued, or when the reason you bought it breaks — prices return to their fundamentals, or even below them. Move it into the undervalued, and keep the 10% cash.

VIX — buy when the VIX is over 30, sell or trim when the VIX is under 15.

Do it yourself

Investing for yourself is a major advantage over handing it to an advisor. Nobody cares about your money the way you do, a yearly fee compounds against you for decades, and doing it yourself is what makes you understand what you own — the first rule of this profile.

Ikigai

Keep a day job you love: work you enjoy, work you’re good at, work people need, that pays for your life. When a job like that carries your life, your investments never have to — and that is what makes an investment process sustainable: nothing ever forces your hand.

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

James Simons (1938–2024), mathematician and former code-breaker, founded Renaissance Technologies; its Medallion Fund averaged about 66% a year gross and about 39% net, 1988–2018. He replaced reading about companies with a scientific search: computers testing whether a price pattern repeats more often than chance can explain.

Entry

The buy rule itself is secret — the patterns, and how strong one must be before the computer acts, have never been published, so no outside number can be stated. What is public is the shape of the machine: it trades only where there are many years of clean price history to test against, and enough daily trading to get in and out within days without moving the price.

Secret signal
Edge

A tiny edge, repeated relentlessly: Renaissance co-CEO Robert Mercer put the share of winning trades at 50.75% — barely better than a coin flip — across 150,000–300,000 trades a day, with positions held 1–2 days to 1–2 weeks.

50.75% hit rate
Risk / Exit

The edge is protected by staying small: Medallion is capped at about $10B, profits are returned to investors every year, outside money was expelled in 2005, and the traders never override the computers.

~$10B capacity cap

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Co-founded PayPal (sold to eBay for $1.5B, 2002) and Palantir (2003); first outside investor in Facebook — $500,000 for 10.2% in 2004, sold for over $1B in 2012. He backs only companies that can become monopolies — the only real player in a small market first — judged by seven questions. A venture framework for startups, not a public-stock screen.

Entry

Buys when a company's own technology is at least 10 times better than its nearest substitute in a dimension that matters — not a little better, an order of magnitude better.

≥10× vs substitute
Edge

A monopoly that strengthens as it grows: each new user makes it more valuable to the others (network effects), serving one more customer costs almost nothing, and the brand cannot be copied.

Principle (not measurable)
Risk / Exit

Avoids any company that cannot answer all seven of his questions: Is the technology a breakthrough, not an improvement? Is now the right time to start it? Does it begin with a big share of a small market? Is the team the right one? Is there a way to reach customers? Will the advantage still stand in 10–20 years? Is it built on a secret — an important truth few people agree with?

Principle (not measurable)

Partner and Senior Managing Director at Yorkville Ives (co-founded July 2026 after eight years as Wedbush Global Head of Technology Research). He is a stock analyst, not a fund manager: his framework is a rating and a 12-month price target, and the rating rests on one bet — a company is a central receiver of the AI buildout's spending.

Entry

Rates a stock Outperform (his buy rating) when the company sits at the centre of the AI buildout — chips, cloud, business software or cybersecurity — with business adoption accelerating. His current top five into 2027, with the 12-month targets he published on 7 Oct 2026: Nvidia $300, Microsoft $615, Palantir $250, Apple $400, CrowdStrike $335. Macro / top-down18 months aheadLiquidity expanding, 18-month outlookLiquidity regime turns / thesis breaksPartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Stanley Druckenmiller founded Duquesne Capital in 1981 and averaged about 30% a year to 2010, with no losing completed calendar year. He invests looking 18 months ahead, following central-bank liquidity — how much money the central banks are putting into the system or taking out of it — not what companies are earning today.

Entry

Buys when that money flow is expanding and the world 18 months ahead looks materially better than today. The direction of the money flow is the test, not a single stock's earnings.

Liquidity expanding
Edge

Bets big only on tremendous conviction, and only when the payoff is lopsided — far more to gain than to lose. In the 1992 pound trade, a position of about $10B risked roughly 0.5–6% against roughly 15–20% upside. And he acts before the proof is complete: "My advantage is not IQ, it's trigger pulling" (Morgan Stanley, 2026).

Asymmetric payoff
Risk / Exit

Sells when the money flow turns or the 18-month story breaks — cutting the position then, rather than waiting for company earnings to confirm it.

Thesis broken = exit

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: Duquesne: ~30% a year, 1981–2010, no losing completed calendar year. Designed the 1992 pound short (~$1B profit); bought Nvidia at ~$150 in 2022 — his trigger was watching Stanford's top talent shift from crypto to AI — and sold in 2024 between $800–$950 (pre-split) — a “big mistake” in his words; the stock hit ~$1,400 five weeks later.
  • Holdings — Q2 2026 13F: $5.2B book, 95 positions: Natera $865M (16.6%), TSMC $282M, STMicroelectronics $232M, Insmed $152M, YPF $143M. No Nvidia.
  • Outlook: “AI is very, very real and could be every bit as impactful as the internet” (Sohn, 2023); by Jan 2026 he called biotech the best AI use case, with AI “no longer driving the engine” of his portfolio.

Value (moats)Long-term (holds)≥10% pre-tax, very high probability; price < intrinsic valueDishonest/incompetent management, undue leverage — PrinciplePartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Berkshire Hathaway's former CEO, whose per-share market value compounded 19.7% a year from 1965–2025, against 10.5% for the S&P 500 with dividends. He buys businesses he can understand, protected by an advantage rivals cannot copy, run by honest and capable managers, at a very attractive price — and then holds them.

Entry

Buys when he sees a very high probability of at least 10% a year before tax, at a price below intrinsic value — what the business is really worth — measured by owner earnings: the cash the business produces after spending what it needs to stay in shape.

≥10% pre-tax, very high probability (2002 letter)
Edge

A moat — an advantage rivals cannot copy — that shows up in the numbers: return on equity (the profit earned on the owners' money in the business) averaging over 20% across 10 years, with no single year below 15%.

ROE >20% avg / ≥15% every year (1987 letter)
Risk / Exit

Sells / avoids when management is dishonest or incompetent, or when the business needs heavy borrowing to earn its returns. He has never stated a debt number — the test is the borrowing the business needs, not a ratio. (Principle — not measurable.)

No debt-to-equity threshold stated (1989 letter)

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: Berkshire: per-share market value compounded 19.7% a year, 1965–2025, vs 10.5% for the S&P 500. Coca-Cola: $1.3B in 1988–94 → ~$32.5B stake at 30 June 2026 (~$37.6B at 30 Oct 2026 close); ~$848M a year in dividends at the 2026 rate ($816M collected in 2025). Apple: ~$35B cost → ~$66B remaining stake (most sold in 2024; $35B became ~$185B pre-tax counting dividends and gains).
  • Holdings — Q2 2026 13F: Apple $66.0B, American Express $51.3B, Alphabet $37.8B combined (GOOGL + GOOG) — the #3 holding, ahead of Coca-Cola $32.5B — Bank of America $27.5B. Cash pile $377.4B (30 Sep 2026).
  • Succession: Stepped down as CEO 1 Jan 2026 (Greg Abel is now President & CEO); stepped down as chairman 18 Sep 2026, becoming Chairman Emeritus — son Howard G. Buffett is chairman.

Macro / risk parity—All Weather 30/40/15/7.5/7.5, rebalanced annuallyLate-cycle debt avoidance; underweight bondsNo

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Ray Dalio founded Bridgewater in 1975 and built Pure Alpha to about 11.4% a year since December 1991 (Bloomberg, July 2022), including +9.5% in 2008, while All Weather returned about 7.8% a year from 1996 to 2019. He treats the economy as a machine of short-term (5–8 year) and long-term (50–75 year) debt cycles, and builds portfolios that survive every kind of economic weather by balancing risk — not by picking stocks.

Entry

Buys a balanced mix, split by risk rather than by dollars — 30% stocks / 40% long-term bonds / 15% intermediate bonds / 7.5% gold / 7.5% commodities — so that each of the four kinds of weather (growth rising or falling, inflation rising or falling) finds part of the portfolio built for it. Rebalanced at least once a year.

Risk parity, not dollars
Edge

Holds 15–20 good return streams — sources of return that move for unrelated reasons — which he says cuts the portfolio's risk by about 80% without cutting the expected return. The test is that the streams genuinely move independently, not how many positions there are.

15–20 streams, ~80% risk cut
Risk / Exit

Avoids debt-heavy assets when the long debt cycle is late and borrowers must start paying debt down instead of rolling it over. On 21 August 2026 his version of that was: underweight bonds, and hold 10–15% in gold plus a bit of Bitcoin.

Underweight debt, 10–15% gold

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: Pure Alpha: ~11.4% a year since December 1991; +9.5% in 2008 while the average hedge fund lost ~18%. Pure Alpha +33% in 2025 is Bridgewater's record under its post-Dalio leadership, not Dalio's. All Weather (risk parity): ~7.8% a year, 1996–2019.
  • Holdings — Q2 2026 13F: $24.38B, 997 positions (equities only — ~$24B against ~$92B firm AUM): SPY $3.97B (16.3%), IVV $2.25B — the two index ETFs alone are 25.5% of the 13F — Nvidia $774M, Broadcom $498M, Amazon $483M.
  • Outlook: “Underweight bonds, hold 10–15% of a portfolio in gold and a bit of Bitcoin” (21 Aug 2026) — a US debt crisis could arrive “in three years, give or take two.”

Distressed value—Distressed claims at 12–20¢ on the dollarValuations far ahead of floor — PrinciplePartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Founder of Appaloosa Management (1993), which returned 132% in 2009 on ~$7–7.5B of profit from distressed bank debt and equity, and was up 32% (gross) in H1 2026. He buys claims that stand at the front of the payment queue at a deep discount when a government backstop or that front-of-queue position limits what he can lose — and buys everything when a central bank or government is easing aggressively.

Entry

Buys when senior or preferred claims — the debts and preferred shares that get paid first if a company fails — trade at 12–20 cents per dollar of face value, or when shares trade at $2–3 against a stated government purchase price of $6. Either way he pays roughly a third to a half of a stated floor price: a margin of safety of roughly 50–67%.

12–20¢ on the dollar
Edge

He reads the rescue terms before the market does. The stated government floor is at least twice the price he pays, so what he can lose is bounded by his place in the queue and by the floor — not by hope.

Floor ≥2x price paid
Risk / Exit

He states no numeric sell trigger. He trims when prices run far ahead of that floor or a rally becomes extreme — he trimmed Micron by 41% in Q2 2026 after a run of more than 300% in half a year, and sold out of SanDisk after a 591% run. (Principle — not measurable.)

No stated trigger

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: 2009: bought bank debt and preferreds at 10–20¢ on the dollar — ~$7–7.5B profit, fund +130–132%. In Sep 2024 told CNBC to “buy everything” in China after the stimulus; Alibaba more than doubled by its Sep–Oct 2025 peak (full-year 2025: +72–82%).
  • Holdings — Q2 2026 13F: $7.47B long equities, 25 positions ($7.72B / 27 positions including options): Amazon $1.19B, Micron $1.13B, TSMC $788M, Alphabet $654M, Uber $555M. Fund +32% (gross) through H1 2026.

Deep value—Margin of safety, up to 50%+ by uncertaintySell at intrinsic value; leverage 0No

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Founder of The Baupost Group (1982), whose largest partnership returned just over 20% a year net since 1983 with only one losing year at that point — a record that has since cooled to about 4% a year since 2014, with five down years in 44 years. He invests for absolute return — making money outright, not just keeping up with an index — by avoiding permanent loss first: buy only at a margin of safety, hold cash when nothing qualifies, and use no borrowed money.

Entry

Buys when the price is at least 50% below a careful, pessimistic estimate of intrinsic value — what the asset is really worth — for uncertain or distressed assets. Where the value is highly certain, the discount can be smaller, but it must still be significant.

Margin of safety up to 50%+ by uncertainty (1991)
Edge

Senior claims (the debts that get paid first if a company fails) and distressed debt bought far below what they would recover, with no leverage — tested by only five down years in 44 years, the worst −12%.

5 down years / worst −12% (2026)
Risk / Exit

Sells when the price rises to his careful estimate of value, so the margin of safety is gone — or avoids anything that would need borrowed money to work.

Sell at intrinsic value; leverage 0

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: Baupost: just over 20% a year net since 1983 with only one losing year at that point (a c. 2012 snapshot of one vehicle) — since then the record has cooled to ~4% a year since 2014, with five down years in 44 years (worst −12%). Author of Margin of Safety (1991); raised ~$4B in 2008 to buy from panicked sellers.
  • Holdings — Q2 2026 13F only ($5.42B — roughly a quarter of Baupost's ~$22–23B total AUM): Amazon $892M (16.5%), Elevance Health $493M, Restaurant Brands $490M, Alphabet $485M, Ferguson $344M.
  • Outlook: June 2026: holding so much cash was something he “almost certainly made a mistake” on. No forward market prediction verified.

Macro (fiscal dominance)—Deficits 5–7% GDP, debt >100% GDP; three pillarsOver-owned/overvalued — PrinciplePartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Founder of Lyn Alden Investment Strategy (2016) and author of Broken Money (2023), with no fund track record — an analyst and author, and a general partner at Ego Death Capital. She invests for the fiscal-dominance regime — a world where the government's borrowing needs, not the central bank, steer the economy — rather than predicting when it arrives.

Entry

Her starting condition: US fiscal deficits running at 5–7% of GDP (the size of the whole economy) with public debt above 100% of GDP. For that world she holds three pillars: profitable equities; commodities, their producers and hard monies (assets no one can print more of, like gold and Bitcoin); and cash equivalents — instead of long-duration bonds, which lock money away for decades and fall hardest when rates rise.

Deficits 5–7% of GDP
Edge

The three pillars cover the three ways the economy can go: profitable equities for growth with slowing inflation; commodities, producers and hard monies for inflation or stagflation (prices rising while the economy stalls); cash equivalents, typically 5–10%, for a credit contraction — the case a standard 60/40 portfolio has no answer for.

Cash typically 5–10%
Risk / Exit

Avoids assets that depend on long-term promises paid in printed money, and leans gradually out of whatever has become over-owned and overvalued, into what is cheap. She states no numeric sell trigger. (Principle — not measurable.)

No stated trigger

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: No fund track record — analyst and author (Broken Money, 2023). Early advocate of the fiscal-dominance framework; long-time holder of gold and Bitcoin.
  • Holdings: Three-pillar portfolio (reiterated June 2026): profitable equities; commodities and hard monies (gold, Bitcoin, energy producers); cash equivalents over long-duration bonds. Personally holds gold and Bitcoin.
  • Outlook: “The fiscal side will win” (29 Sep 2026) — ~$10T of US deficits over the next five years. On Bitcoin: Milk Road (26–27 Oct 2026) — base case the bottom “is in”, but “a bottom does not mean an immediate rally”; Kitco (29 Sep 2026) — Bitcoin “near the low end of its valuation and sentiment range” (~$72,660), no major rally called in the next ~3 months.

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

30+ year Wall Street veteran — Morgan Stanley managing director, founding partner of Anchor Point, and Weiss Multi-Strategy president & CIO 2005–2024 — now head of AI Macro Nexus at 22V Research and founder of Visser Labs (2024). He invests where the AI building money flows: to the companies that physically receive the spending. He also treats crypto as the payment rails for AI agents.

Entry

Buys when the hyperscalers — the handful of giant companies building AI data centres — are raising their capital spending (capex: money spent building) year on year, and the company receives that spending in the bottom layers of his five-layer stack: energy, chips and computing, networking and storage — rather than selling software on top.

CapEx receivers
Edge

The big indexes still weight the last era's software winners most heavily, so the physical inputs to AI are under-owned until the indexes catch up. He tracks the gap in his 100-stock AI portfolio (up about 40% in 2026 to October) and his thematic basket (up 34% since November 2024).

Benchmark arbitrage
Risk / Exit

Sells when the AI trade gets crowded — he began trimming Micron in mid-May 2026 after hedge funds and retail piled in — or when a spender's building budget outruns the cash its business generates and is funded with debt, as with Oracle's $55.7B of capex against $32B of operating cash flow in fiscal 2026.

Quant (factors) + venture≥1 yearCheapest decile + top 25–50 six-month momentumQuality-screen fail / faded factor rankPartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, son of quant pioneer James O'Shaughnessy, ran his father's firm OSAM as CEO from 2018 until its sale to Franklin Templeton (announced 2021, completed January 2022; $6.5 billion AUM). In public stocks he never picks by opinion: a fixed system of tests ranks every stock, and he buys only what passes. (His venture firm Positive Sum, which put $20 million into Tegus before its $930 million acquisition by AlphaSense in 2024, is a separate business and is not scored here.)

Entry

A stock must rank in the cheapest 10% of its universe on Value Composite Two — six price ratios combined into one cheapness score — and among the top 25–50 names on six-month momentum: how strongly its price has risen over the last six months.

Entry · Cheapest decile + top 6-month momentum
Edge

Six tests, none of them his opinion. Three select: cheapness, momentum, and shareholder yield (the cash a company returns to its shareholders for each share). Three reject: financial strength, earnings quality and earnings growth flag companies that are poor quality despite a cheap price. The 45-year backtest of the system (1964–2009) returned 21.19% a year against 11.22% for the average stock.

Edge · Six-factor system; backtested 1964–2009
Risk / Exit

Sells at the scheduled rebalance when a holding's quality tests flag it as a poor company, or when its ranking fades — typically holding each name at least one year. The model decides, not discretion.

Exit · Quality-screen fail or faded factor rank

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: Positive Sum put $20M into Tegus, acquired by AlphaSense for $930M in 2024 (closed 8 Jul 2024). Portfolio includes Etched, Cognition, Physical Intelligence, Vanta, ID.me, Base Power and Imprint.

AI-stack / bottleneck—P/E gap — scored here via PEGDebt-funded buildout; TSMC ends wafer shortagePartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Gavin Baker is the founder and CIO of Atreides Management, who ran Fidelity's $17 billion OTC fund for eight years (2009–2017), compounding roughly 19.3% a year net of fees and beating over 99% of Morningstar peers. He buys the physical bottlenecks of the AI buildout — watts (electricity), wafers (the silicon discs chips are printed on) and memory — where supply cannot expand to meet demand, and only when the cheap side of that chain is priced far below the expensive side.

Entry

Buys the cheap side of a wide price gap inside the AI chain. In May 2026 he put numbers on it: memory (DRAM) traded at a mid-single-digit multiple of its earnings — roughly 5–9 times — while chip-making equipment traded at about 40 times earnings and optical names at over 100 times. (A multiple is the price divided by one year's earnings: 40 times means paying $40 for each $1 of yearly earnings.)

Cross-sectional valuation
Edge

He owns the bottleneck only while supply cannot expand to meet demand — tested by sold-out capacity, rising prices and full utilisation, with every GPU (the processor AI runs on) running at 100% in May 2026. He learned supply and demand covering cement and aggregates.

Physical bottleneck
Risk / Exit

Sells when the AI buildout starts being funded with debt rather than the operating cash flow of the spenders, or when TSMC expands capacity enough to end the wafer shortage — his single watch-item. When the facts disprove the thesis he sells and accepts the loss; a falling price alone is not a reason.

Funding & capacity

Macro / Bitcoin—Reserves <10% GDP + RRP drainedNo stated exit test — PrincipleNo

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

James Lavish, CFA, is a macro / Bitcoin strategist — not a stock picker — with 30+ years on Wall Street, co-founder and managing partner of the Bitcoin Opportunity Fund, author of The Informationist since 2021, and a Strive (ASST) board director. His approach in one line: own assets no government can print, because a government debt load that cannot be repaid leaves debasing the currency as the only politically survivable way out.

Entry

Buys when bank reserves fall below 10% of GDP (the size of the whole economy) while the Fed's reverse-repo facility — the overnight parking place where banks leave spare cash with the Fed — is effectively drained. That is his signal that quantitative tightening (the Fed taking money out of the system) must end and quantitative easing (the Fed putting money in) must follow. In October 2025 the readings were 9.71% and about $5B.

Test: reserves / GDP; RRP balance — Oct 2025: 9.71% and ~$5B
Edge

Bitcoin's fixed cap of 21 million, which no government, central bank, company or miner can raise — against gold, whose supply grows about 1.5–2% a year as new metal is mined.

Test: protocol supply cap of 21M vs gold's annual mining growth
Risk / Exit

He has stated no sell price or exit condition for Bitcoin. His $400,000–$500,000 figure for mid-2029 is a power-law forecast — a price path fitted to Bitcoin's history — not a sell rule, and he expects a 60–70% drawdown after any such peak. (Principle — not measurable.)

No stated exit test; forecast only

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: Co-founded the Bitcoin Opportunity Fund on this thesis; appointed to the board of Strive, Inc. (Nasdaq: ASST) — SEC Form 3, 12 Sep 2025, shows Bitcoin Opportunity Fund vehicles holding 759,259 + 231,852 + 120,000 ASST Class A shares. No audited fund return found.
  • Outlook: Bitcoin $400,000–$500,000 by mid-2029 (power-law forecast, What Bitcoin Did, 30 Oct 2026; repeated BMTV, 10–11 Nov 2026) — a lowered base case vs his earlier $1M by 2030/2031; he “would be absolutely shocked” if Bitcoin were not $200,000–$300,000 by then. His $150K–$180K call for 2026 had not materialised by Nov 2026 (BTC ~$73K). He expects a 60–70% drawdown after any such peak.

Venture (SaaS) + policy—CMGR ≥15%/≥10%; retention ≥100%; gross margin ≥75%Burn Multiple >2; retention <100%; margin <75%No

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Venture investor and policy advocate — not a stock picker. PayPal's first product leader, then COO (1999–2002; eBay acquired PayPal for $1.5B); co-founded Yammer, sold to Microsoft for $1.2B in cash in 2012; co-founded Craft Ventures in late 2017; White House AI & Crypto Czar, 20 Jan 2025–26 Mar 2026. His testable framework is Craft's published screen for subscription software sold to businesses: buy only software that spreads on its own, keeps its customers spending, and burns little cash for each new dollar of revenue.

Entry

Buys when a company grows at a compound monthly rate of at least 15% while its ARR — annual recurring revenue, its subscription income counted for a full year — is below $1M, and at least 10% once ARR is above $1M; when its existing customers spend at least as much as they did last year (dollar retention of at least 100%); and when its gross margin — what remains of each sales dollar after the direct cost of serving customers — is at least 75%.

Craft, "The SaaS Metrics That Matter" — Series A bar
Edge

Bottom-up software: a product workers adopt inside a company the way they adopt a consumer app, before any executive buys it. His engagement test is at least 40% DAU/MAU — of the people who use it in a month, at least 40% use it on any given day. Yammer's own proof: 0 to 5M users and 85% of the Fortune 500 in under four years.

Craft, "Announcing Craft III" (2021); Yammer, 2008–2012
Risk / Exit

Avoids companies whose Burn Multiple — the cash burned divided by the net new ARR gained — rises above 2, whose customers spend less than last year (retention below 100%), or whose gross margin stays below 75%.

Sacks, Burn Multiple (Apr 2020); Craft SaaS benchmarks

Top Investments, Holdings & Outlook

  • Top investments: PayPal (first product leader, then COO; eBay acquired it for $1.5B, Oct 2002); Yammer, co-founded with Adam Pisoni, sold to Microsoft for $1.2B cash in 2012; Craft Ventures Fund I $350M (2018); angel investor in Facebook, Uber, SpaceX, Palantir and Airbnb (check sizes and dates not publicly disclosed).
  • Holdings: Craft Ventures — $3.3B AUM at Nov 2023 (stale; Craft Ventures V filed with the SEC 7 Aug 2026, target ~$1B). No 13F — a venture fund, not a public-stock portfolio. Also COO of Zenefits (Dec 2014) and interim CEO (Feb 2016, ~10 months); co-host of the All-In podcast.
  • Outlook: White House AI & Crypto Czar, 20 Jan 2025–26 Mar 2026 (130 SGE days), then PCAST co-chair (ex officio from Jan 2025). Divested >$200M in crypto-related holdings before taking office (Mar 2025).

Venture (startups)—Software company attacking an uneaten industry — PrincipleNo extreme strength / check-box deal — PrincipleNo

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Co-founded Netscape — IPO August 1995 at $28, closing $58.25 for a ~$2.9B valuation, sold to AOL for $4.2B in stock in 1998 — and Opsware, sold to HP for about $1.6B in 2007; co-founded Andreessen Horowitz in 2009 with a $300M first fund, now about $90B under management. He backs software companies attacking industries software has not eaten yet. A venture investor and policy advocate, not a public-stock screen.

Entry

Buys when a startup is a software company attacking a large industry software has not yet eaten, and it has one extreme strength — one dimension where it is an outlier — even if it is weak elsewhere. His name for the test is "strength versus lack of weakness" (2014): being merely good at everything fails it.

Principle (not measurable)
Edge

The power law: about 15 of the roughly 4,000 venture-fundable companies a year reach $100M in revenue, and those few generate about 97% of all venture returns. So he sizes for the outlier and accepts that most bets fail.

15 of ~4,000; ~97% of returns
Risk / Exit

Avoids companies with no extreme strength and no software edge over their industry — "check-box" deals, reasonable on every dimension and remarkable on none. He states no numeric sell trigger; venture positions are held to an IPO or an acquisition. (Principle — not measurable.)

Principle (not measurable)

Credit / distressed debt—Price below intrinsic value, margin of safety — PrincipleEuphoria / thin risk premiums / no perceived risk — PrincipleNo

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Co-founded Oaktree Capital Management in 1995 with Bruce Karsh, after running high-yield and distressed debt at TCW (1985–1995) and Citicorp (1969–1985); Oaktree stated $209B under management as of 30 June 2025. He has written around 160 public investor memos since October 1990 — "bubble.com" (January 2000) warned of the dot-com bust. He buys credit — the bonds and loans of troubled companies — below what he judges them to be worth when other investors are fearful, and waits when they are euphoric. His method is judgment, not measurement: he publishes no numeric rules. These are the five questions his published work asks of any investment:

  1. Second-level thinking — is my view both different from the crowd's and right? (First-level thinking says "good company, buy it"; second-level asks what is already in the price.)
  2. Price against value — is the price below what it is worth, with a margin of safety?
  3. Cycle position — where are we in the swing between fear and euphoria?
  4. Permanent-loss risk — what is the chance of losing money for good? For Marks that, not price movement, is the only risk that counts.
  5. Knowability — can this actually be known, or is it a guess about the future dressed up as analysis?
Entry

Buys when the price is below his estimate of intrinsic value — what the asset is really worth — with a margin of safety, most often the bonds and loans of troubled companies at a deep discount, on the bet that what they would recover is more than the price.

Principle (not measurable)
Risk / Exit

Refrains when the swing reaches euphoria — prices above value, investors barely paid extra for taking risk (thin risk premiums), and a widespread belief that there is no risk. He prepares rather than predicts, waiting for the cycle to turn. He states no numeric sell trigger. (Judgment — not measured.)

Principle (not measurable)
Growth (fast growers)Years (10–20-year story)Fast grower, PEG < 1.0 at 20–25% growthPEG ≥ 2, growth slows sharply, or story breaksPartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Peter Lynch managed Fidelity's Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, compounding about 29.2% a year and growing its assets from about $18 million to about $14 billion, beating the S&P 500 in 11 of those 13 years. He buys understandable fast-growing companies at a P/E no higher than their growth rate — a PEG of 1 or less — and holds them until the story changes.

Entry

Buys when a fast grower — earnings growing 20–25% a year — trades at a PEG below 1.0, meaning its P/E is below its growth rate; a PEG around 0.5 is very attractive. The PEG test applies only where growth is 15% or more, never to slow growers.

PEG < 1.0, growth 20–25% (1989)
Edge

the tenbagger — small, profitable, understandable companies in dull, overlooked industries, bought before Wall Street notices them; his Dunkin' Donuts stake returned 10–15 times his money.

10–15x on Dunkin' Donuts (1994)
Risk / Exit

Sells / avoids when a fast grower's P/E rises to twice its growth rate (PEG ≥ 2), when its growth slows sharply, or when the story behind the buy breaks — and avoids companies loaded with bank debt, which is due on demand and decides who survives a crisis.

PEG ≥ 2 = sell (fast growers)
Value (defensive)—P/E ≤ 15, P/B ≤ 1.5; net-net ≤ ⅔ NCAVPrice above Graham Number; fails strength testsPartly

Accomplishments & Quantifiable Framework

Columbia professor who wrote Security Analysis (1934, with David Dodd) and The Intelligent Investor (1949, revised 1973); taught Warren Buffett at Columbia and ran the Graham-Newman partnership; his best investment was GEICO. He invented security analysis and the margin of safety — "the central concept of investment" — and buys only at a price far below value, never for growth at any price.

Entry

For the defensive investor, a stock must pass every test on his list:
— the company is substantial (in his day, sales of $100M or more);
— its current ratio is at least 2 (short-term assets at least twice short-term debts), and long-term debt is below net current assets;
— it earned a profit in each of the last 10 years, and paid dividends for 20 years;
— earnings grew by at least a third over 10 years;
— the price is no more than 15 times average earnings of the last three years (P/E ≤ 15) and no more than 1.5 times book value (P/B ≤ 1.5) — or the two multiplied together come to no more than 22.5.

For the enterprising investor, the simpler test: the price is below two-thirds of net current asset value — current assets minus all debts. He called such stocks net-nets.

P/E ≤15, P/B ≤1.5; net-net ≤⅔ NCAV
Edge

The margin of safety. "Confronted with a challenge to distill the secret of sound investment into three words, we venture the motto, MARGIN OF SAFETY" (The Intelligent Investor, ch. 20) — a gap large enough that "it is enough to assume that future earnings will not fall far below those of the past."

Margin of safety (1949)
Risk / Exit

Sells when the price rises above the Graham Number — the highest price his formula allows: the square root of 22.5 × earnings per share × book value per share — or when a holding fails the financial-strength tests. He never pays up for growth and never buys on a forecast.

Graham Number = √(22.5 × EPS × BVPS)

Where My Investor Committee Agrees: A Short Checklist

Eighteen investors, from venture to macro to quant to value — and they agree on almost nothing specific. What follows is what survives the test.

  1. Follow a written process — and decide in advance what would change your mind.
  2. Know why you own it — be able to explain the thesis in a sentence or two.
  3. Hold cash when nothing meets your bar — cash is a position, not a failure.

The Benner Cycle — “Periods When to Make Money”

Samuel Benner’s three lines, redrawn from his card — every year exactly as the card prints it. The full card runs from 1780 to 2059; this redraw shows the years from 1924 on.

A“Years in which panics have occurred and will occur again.”

B“Years of Good Times, High Prices and the time to sell Stocks and values of all kinds.”

C“Years of Hard Times, Low Prices, and a good time to buy Stocks, “Corner Lots,” Goods, etc., and hold till the “Boom” reaches the years of good times; then unload.”

The card claims the market moves in three repeating rhythms — the three lines above, in the card’s own words. Its footer promises: “‘Sure thing.’ Save this card and watch it closely.”

Samuel Benner (1832–1913) was an Ohio farmer, an accountant, and a Civil War veteran. The Panic of 1873 — combined with an outbreak of hog cholera — wiped him out financially, and he went looking for the pattern in prices. In 1875 he published Benner’s Prophecies of Future Ups and Downs in Prices: What Years to Make Money on Pig-Iron, Hogs, Corn, and Provisions, built on United States government price records running from 1780 to 1872. The book was reprinted in sixteen updated editions through 1907, and the chart outlived it: printers gave it away on trade cards — the Denver hardware card above is one — and it has been reprinted ever since.

Its record is mixed, and this page keeps it as history, not as a rule. Some of the card’s years landed near real turns; many did not, and the lines have never been shown to predict prices. The Investor Committee above runs on published rules and evidence — Benner is here because no history of market lore is complete without him.

Read strictly as the card reads, its line for the present is this: the B line — good times, the time to sell — includes 2026. The C line’s most recent buy year was 2023. The A line’s next panic year is 2035. Those are the card’s claims, set in type in the 1800s — not advice.
